`notification show` uses the configured `[ui.toast]` delivery. `--position` only affects in-app Herdr toasts. `--sound` defaults to `none`; `done` and `request` play the existing finished and needs-attention sounds only when the notification is shown.

## Sessions

```bash
herdr session list [--json]
herdr session attach <name>
herdr session stop <name> [--json]
herdr session delete <name> [--json]
```

Use `default` as the session name when you need to stop the default session explicitly.

## Workspaces

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr workspace create [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]
herdr workspace get <workspace_id>
herdr workspace focus <workspace_id>
herdr workspace rename <workspace_id> <label>
herdr workspace report-metadata <workspace_id> --source ID [--token NAME=VALUE] [--clear-token NAME] [--seq N] [--ttl-ms N]
herdr workspace close <workspace_id>
```

Create a workspace without stealing focus:

```bash
herdr workspace create --cwd ~/project --label api --no-focus
```

A workspace is a top-level project or work context. Creating one also creates its first tab and root pane. The JSON response exposes their IDs as `.result.workspace.workspace_id`, `.result.tab.tab_id`, and `.result.root_pane.pane_id`.

## Worktrees

```bash
herdr worktree list [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH]
herdr worktree create [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--branch NAME] [--base REF] [--path PATH] [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus]
herdr worktree open [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] (--path PATH | --branch NAME) [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus]
herdr worktree remove --workspace ID [--force]
```

Worktrees are normal Herdr workspaces with Git checkout provenance. `worktree create` creates a Git worktree checkout, opens it as a workspace, and groups it with the parent repo workspace. If `--branch` names an existing local branch, Herdr checks it out; otherwise it creates the branch from `--base` or `HEAD`. Without `--path`, Herdr creates the checkout under `<worktrees.directory>/<repo>/<branch-slug>`.

`workspace close` closes only Herdr state. To delete the checkout, run `worktree remove`. It runs `git worktree remove`, never deletes the branch, and requires `--force` when Git refuses a dirty checkout.

## Tabs

```bash
herdr tab list [--workspace <workspace_id>]
herdr tab create [--workspace <workspace_id>] [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]
herdr tab get <tab_id>
herdr tab focus <tab_id>
herdr tab rename <tab_id> <label>
herdr tab close <tab_id>
```

A tab is another terminal layout inside a workspace. Without `--workspace`, `tab create` uses the active workspace and fails if none exists. Its JSON response exposes `.result.tab.tab_id` and `.result.root_pane.pane_id`. Closing a workspace's last tab also closes the workspace, matching the TUI close-tab action. If `confirm_close` is enabled and closing the tab would also close a whole worktree group, `tab close` returns a `confirmation_required` error instead.

Workspace and tab creation, and pane splitting, leave focus unchanged by default. `--focus` selects the new layout; `--no-focus` states the default explicitly. Without `--cwd`, new terminals follow the configured `terminal.new_cwd` policy, which follows the source pane or workspace by default. Each `--env KEY=VALUE` adds or replaces that variable in the new root shell.

## Agents

For the pane-versus-agent model and complete orchestration examples, see [Agent automation](/docs/agent-automation/).

```bash
herdr agent list
herdr agent get <target>
herdr agent read <target> [--source visible|recent|recent-unwrapped|detection] [--lines N] [--format text|ansi] [--ansi]
herdr agent send-keys <target> <key> [key ...]
herdr agent prompt <target> <text> [--wait] [--until STATUS]... [--timeout MS]
herdr agent rename <target> <name>|--clear
herdr agent focus <target>
herdr agent wait <target> [--until STATUS]... [--timeout MS]
herdr agent attach <target> [--takeover]
herdr agent start <name> --kind KIND --pane ID [--timeout MS] [-- <agent-args...>]
herdr agent explain <target> [--json|--verbose]
herdr agent explain --file PATH --agent LABEL [--json|--verbose]
```

Agent targets are either a unique live agent name or the pane ID that currently hosts the agent. Terminal IDs and bare agent-kind labels are not agent targets. Agents started through `agent start` require a name; manually launched agents remain unnamed and use their pane ID.

`agent start` activates an existing available shell pane: the pane's interactive shell must own the foreground, with no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Topology must be created separately. Names are unique among live agents and must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}`. The kind selects Herdr's canonical interactive executable, while arguments after `--` are passed to that executable. Supported kinds are `pi`, `claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `cursor`, `devin`, `agy`, `cline`, `omp`, `mastracode`, `opencode`, `copilot`, `kimi`, `kiro`, `droid`, `amp`, `grok`, `hermes`, `kilo`, `qodercli`, and `maki`. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced. Temporary detection uncertainty does not clear it.

A successful start returns only after the expected agent owns the same terminal and is ready for interactive input. If detection reports `blocked` during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately. The name remains available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`, and becomes ready for prompts after detection reports `idle`. The default startup timeout is 30000 milliseconds; explicit values must be greater than 3000 and no more than 300000.

`agent prompt` honors live bracketed-paste mode and submits text plus encoded Enter atomically, including while the agent is working. With `--wait`, a prompt sent from a non-working state must produce an observed lifecycle change within five seconds or Herdr returns `agent_prompt_stalled`; a caller timeout of five seconds or less keeps the normal `timeout` error. After activity is observed, it waits for the first requested settled status. It does not track individual turns. If the agent is already working, completion of that active turn may satisfy the wait. `--until` narrows the matching states and is rejected unless `--wait` is also present. Standalone `agent wait` returns immediately when the current status matches. Both default to `idle`, `done`, or `blocked`; use `--until unknown` explicitly when needed.

`idle` means ready for input after its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI; `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work completes. Focusing that tab or targeting it with `pane focus` / `agent focus` marks it seen; reading it through the CLI does not. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently, not that its work succeeded.

`agent send-keys` sends logical terminal keys such as `enter`, `up`, `esc`, or `ctrl+c`. Herdr validates every key before writing any bytes. `agent read` reads the resolved terminal stream, and `agent rename` names an already detected agent.

`agent explain` asks the running server to classify the same bottom-buffer detection snapshot used by screen detection, so live output reflects the server's active manifest cache. Because this uses the `agent.explain` socket method, restart or hand off to an updated server after upgrading Herdr before using live explain. Use `--file PATH --agent LABEL` to explain a saved fixture locally instead. The default output shows the agent, final state, manifest source and version, matched rule with its region evidence, and any fallback, skip, or warning reasons. Add `--verbose` for visible evidence flags, cached remote version, local override shadowing, remote update status, and the full evaluated-rules list with matcher and region evidence. Add `--json` for issue reports or tests.

Use `pane send-text`, `pane send-keys`, `pane run`, and `terminal attach` for ordinary terminals, servers, tests, shells, or low-level terminal control. Use `pane run` when you want to submit a command with Enter.

## Plugins

Plugin commands install and run local executable workflow plugins. A plugin is a manifest plus out-of-process commands; Herdr owns the host surface and plugins own their implementation language.

Install, list, and remove plugins:

```bash
herdr plugin install <owner>/<repo>[/subdir...] [--ref REF] [--yes]
herdr plugin list [--plugin ID] [--json]
herdr plugin uninstall <plugin_id|owner/repo[/subdir...]>
herdr plugin enable <plugin_id>
herdr plugin disable <plugin_id>
```

`plugin install` accepts GitHub shorthand only, such as `ogulcancelik/herdr-plugin-examples/worktree-bootstrap`. It uses `git`, shows a trust preview in interactive terminals, runs supported manifest build commands, and stores GitHub installs in a Herdr-managed directory. Use `--yes` for noninteractive installs. Reinstalling a GitHub-managed plugin replaces that managed checkout. Installing over a locally linked plugin is refused. Plugin manifests must declare `min_herdr_version`; install and link fail when the plugin requires a newer Herdr binary. `plugin list` is human-readable by default; pass `--json` for the raw API response.

Plugin installation and enabled state are global to the current user. A plugin installed, linked, enabled, or disabled through one Herdr session is immediately available with the same state in every session.

Local development:

```bash
herdr plugin link <path> [--disabled]
herdr plugin unlink <plugin_id>
```

`plugin link` accepts a plugin directory containing `herdr-plugin.toml` or a direct manifest path. Use it while authoring or testing a plugin from a local checkout. `plugin unlink` unregisters the plugin and leaves files alone. `plugin uninstall` unregisters a plugin and also removes Herdr-managed GitHub checkout files. For GitHub installs, uninstall accepts either the plugin id or the same `owner/repo[/subdir...]` shorthand used by install. Actions, event hooks, panes, and link handlers are declared in the manifest; runtime action registration is not part of v1.

```bash
herdr plugin config-dir <plugin_id>

Actions:

```bash
herdr plugin action list [--plugin ID]
herdr plugin action invoke <action_id> [--plugin ID]

`plugin action invoke` starts the manifest command for an installed, enabled,
platform-compatible plugin action and prints the started command log record in
the JSON response. Use the qualified action id (`plugin.id.action`) when more
than one plugin uses the same action id. Local action ids cannot contain dots,
so qualified ids remain unambiguous even when plugin ids contain dots.

herdr plugin log list [--plugin ID] [--limit N]

content.text:
I've read through herdr's plugin system, its worktree APIs, and entire's trail commands. Here's what I found before I start building.

## What herdr gives you

**Worktree primitives (CLI + socket, both usable from a plugin):**
- `herdr worktree create --branch X [--base REF] [--cwd parent-repo] [--label] [--focus]` — creates the checkout under `~/.herdr/worktrees/<repo>/<slug>`, opens it as a workspace, groups it with the parent repo workspace
- `herdr worktree open --cwd <parent> --path <existing-worktree>` — *adopts* a worktree created by someone else, same grouping/labeling
- Both return `.result.root_pane.pane_id`, which feeds `herdr agent start <name> --kind claude --pane <id>`, then optionally `herdr agent prompt <name> "<text>"`

**Plugin system** (`docs/next/website/src/content/docs/plugins.mdx`): a directory with `herdr-plugin.toml` + any argv command. The whole herdr CLI *is* the plugin API (`HERDR_BIN_PATH`). Relevant surfaces:
- `[[actions]]` bound to keys via `[[keys.command]] type = "plugin_action"`
- `[[link_handlers]]` — a regex on clicked terminal URLs → routes ctrl+click to an action, with `HERDR_PLUGIN_CLICKED_URL` in the env. A trail URL (`https://entire.io/gh/owner/repo/trails/575/slug`) matches cleanly
- `[[panes]] placement = "popup"` — a session-modal terminal popup that gets all input. This is the only way to get a "paste something here" prompt; **plugin actions take no arguments**, and plugins have zero native UI surface (no entries in herdr's menus or the sidebar — `src/ui/` has no plugin references at all)
- `HERDR_PLUGIN_CONTEXT_JSON` carries `selected_text`, `clicked_url`, workspace cwd, worktree info

## What entire already gives you

`entire trail checkout <n> --worktree` (on `main`, in `trail_checkout_worktree.go` — **not** in your installed binary yet) already does most of the hard part: resolves trail → branch, fetches a remote-only branch into `refs/heads`, creates the worktree, copies gitignored files matching `.worktreeinclude`, is idempotent on re-run, and prints the bare path on stdout when not a TTY. It puts checkouts at `<repo>/.entire/worktrees/trail-N-<branch>`, though — not herdr's directory.

Two gaps to close either way: trail selectors accept number/id/branch but **not URLs** (needs parsing), and herdr's own `worktree create --branch` only checks *local* refs — for a remote-only trail branch it would silently create a new branch from HEAD instead, so a fetch (or `--base origin/<branch>`) has to happen first.

Three decisions fork the implementation:

questions.question: Where should the trail→worktree logic live?

options.label: Herdr plugin only (Recommended)
options.description: Self-contained plugin (shell or Go) that shells out to `entire` + `herdr`. Ships and iterates independently, installable by anyone via `herdr plugin install`, no entire release needed. Downside: logic lives outside entire's test suite.

options.label: Split: entire does work, plugin is glue
options.description: Add herdr awareness to the entire CLI (e.g. `entire trail checkout --worktree --open-in-herdr`), so the resolve/fetch/copy logic stays in Go with tests; the plugin is a thin keybinding + popup wrapper. Downside: couples entire to herdr, needs an entire release.

options.label: Fork/patch herdr natively
options.description: Add a native modal alongside the existing 'new worktree' dialog in Rust. Best UX fidelity, but it's a third-party product and a trail-specific feature is unlikely to be upstreamed — you'd carry a fork.

questions.question: Where should the trail worktree checkout live?

options.label: Herdr's directory (Recommended)
options.description: `~/.herdr/worktrees/<repo>/<branch-slug>` via `herdr worktree create`. Matches your existing worktrees, herdr owns removal via `worktree remove`. Plugin must fetch remote-only branches itself and replicate `.worktreeinclude` copying.

options.label: Entire's directory, herdr adopts it
options.description: `entire trail checkout <n> --worktree` then `herdr worktree open --path`. Reuses entire's fetch, `.worktreeinclude` copying, and idempotency for free. Checkouts sit at `<repo>/.entire/worktrees/trail-N-branch`, inconsistent with your other herdr worktrees.

options.label: Configurable, default herdr
options.description: Plugin config picks the base directory; default to herdr's. More code, but no lock-in either way.

questions.question: How do you want to trigger it? (pick all that apply)

options.label: Keybinding → popup prompt
options.description: e.g. `prefix+t` opens a modal terminal popup: paste a trail id or URL, optionally pick the agent, Enter. Closest to the native 'new worktree' modal feel.

options.label: Ctrl+click a trail URL
options.description: A `[[link_handlers]]` regex on `https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<n>` — ctrl+click any trail URL printed in a terminal and it builds the worktree. Zero typing.

options.label: Popup lists open trails
options.description: The popup also lists open trails from `entire trail list --json` so you can arrow-select instead of pasting. Also works from a repo you have no URL for.

options.label: Plain CLI command
options.description: A script/shell function you can call from any pane or from an agent: `herdr-trail 575 --agent claude`. No keybinding needed, scriptable, and easy to test.

name = "Entire Trail Worktree"

[[actions]]
id = "new"

# no native UI surface in Herdr.

id = "prompt"

placement = "popup"
width = "72%"

# Action entrypoint. Runs headless when the keybinding fires: resolves the repo
# the popup should work against, then opens the popup pane.
set -u

herdr="${HERDR_BIN_PATH:-herdr}"

fail() {
	"$herdr" notification show "New worktree from trail" --body "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1
	echo "$1" >&2
	exit 1
}

context="${HERDR_PLUGIN_CONTEXT_JSON:-}"
[ -n "$context" ] || fail "no invocation context"

command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || fail "jq is required (brew install jq)"

# worktree.repo_root is the main checkout even when the action fires from a
# linked worktree workspace; Herdr refuses worktree actions rooted in one.
repo_root=$(printf '%s' "$context" | jq -r '.worktree.repo_root // empty')
if [ -z "$repo_root" ]; then
	cwd=$(printf '%s' "$context" | jq -r '.workspace_cwd // .focused_pane_cwd // empty')
	[ -n "$cwd" ] || fail "no workspace directory in context"
	repo_root=$(git -C "$cwd" rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null) ||
		fail "not a git repository: $cwd"
	repo_root=${repo_root%/.git}
fi

[ -d "$repo_root" ] || fail "repo root not found: $repo_root"

# selected_text lets you highlight a trail URL and hit the key: the popup
# pre-fills it instead of asking.
selection=$(printf '%s' "$context" | jq -r '.selected_text // .clicked_url // empty' | head -n 1)

exec "$herdr" plugin pane open \
	--plugin entire.trail-worktree \
	--entrypoint prompt \
	--placement popup \
	--env "ETW_REPO_ROOT=$repo_root" \
	--env "ETW_PREFILL=$selection"

#!/bin/sh
# Popup entrypoint. Owns terminal input, so this is where the trail id/URL gets
# pasted. Resolves the trail to its branch, creates (or re-opens) the Herdr
# worktree workspace for that branch, and starts an agent in its root pane.
set -u

herdr="${HERDR_BIN_PATH:-herdr}"
entire="${ENTIRE_BIN_PATH:-entire}"
repo_root="${ETW_REPO_ROOT:-}"
prefill="${ETW_PREFILL:-}"
state_dir="${HERDR_PLUGIN_STATE_DIR:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}}"
err_log="$state_dir/last-error.log"

# Config: $(herdr plugin config-dir entire.trail-worktree)/config.env
AGENT_KINDS="claude codex none"
AGENT_DEFAULT="claude"
INITIAL_PROMPT=""
config_file="${HERDR_PLUGIN_CONFIG_DIR:-}/config.env"
if [ -n "${HERDR_PLUGIN_CONFIG_DIR:-}" ] && [ -f "$config_file" ]; then
	# shellcheck disable=SC1090
	. "$config_file"
fi

if [ -t 1 ]; then
	bold=$(printf '\033[1m')
	dim=$(printf '\033[2m')
	red=$(printf '\033[31m')
	green=$(printf '\033[32m')
	reset=$(printf '\033[0m')
else
	bold=''
	dim=''
	red=''
	green=''
	reset=''
fi
esc=$(printf '\033')

step() { printf '  %s%s%s\n' "$dim" "$1" "$reset"; }
ok() { printf '  %s✓%s %s\n' "$green" "$reset" "$1"; }

die() {
	printf '\n  %serror%s %s\n' "$red" "$reset" "$1"
	if [ -s "$err_log" ]; then
		sed -n '1,6p' "$err_log" | sed "s/^/  $dim/;s/\$/$reset/"
	fi
	printf '\n  press enter to close '
	read -r _ || true
	exit 1
}

# Herdr CLI calls print a JSON envelope; a failed call carries .error.
check_response() {
	message=$(printf '%s' "$1" | jq -r '.error.message // .error.code // empty' 2>/dev/null)
	[ -z "$message" ] || die "$2: $message"
}

: >"$err_log" 2>/dev/null || err_log=/dev/null

[ -n "$repo_root" ] || die "no repo root supplied"
cd "$repo_root" 2>/dev/null || die "cannot enter $repo_root"
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "jq is required (brew install jq)"
command -v "$entire" >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "'entire' not found on PATH"

origin=$(git remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null) ||
	die "no origin remote in $repo_root"
origin_slug=$(printf '%s' "$origin" | sed -e 's#\.git$##' -e 's#^.*[:/]\([^/]*/[^/]*\)$#\1#')

printf '\n  %snew worktree from trail%s  %s%s%s\n\n' \
	"$bold" "$reset" "$dim" "$origin_slug" "$reset"

if [ -n "$prefill" ]; then
	printf '  trail %s[%s]%s: ' "$dim" "$prefill" "$reset"
else
	printf '  trail %s(number, id, branch, or URL)%s: ' "$dim" "$reset"
fi
IFS= read -r input || exit 0
case "$input" in "$esc"*) exit 0 ;; esac
[ -n "$input" ] || input="$prefill"
[ -n "$input" ] || exit 0

# A pasted URL (https://entire.io/gh/owner/repo/trails/992/slug) carries both the
# trail number and the repo it belongs to. The repo has to match this checkout:
# resolving a foreign trail here would silently check out the wrong branch.
selector=$input
case "$input" in
*/trails/*)
	path=${input#*://}
	path=${path#*/}
	before=${path%%/trails/*}
	after=${path#*/trails/}
	number=${after%%/*}
	number=${number%%\?*}
	number=${number%%#*}
	url_owner=${before%/*}
	url_owner=${url_owner##*/}
	url_repo=${before##*/}
	url_slug="$url_owner/$url_repo"

	case "$number" in
	'' | *[!0-9]*) die "could not read a trail number from $input" ;;
	esac
	lower_url=$(printf '%s' "$url_slug" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
	lower_origin=$(printf '%s' "$origin_slug" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
	if [ "$lower_url" != "$lower_origin" ]; then
		die "that trail belongs to $url_slug, but this workspace is $origin_slug"
	fi
	selector=$number
	;;
esac

step "resolving trail $selector…"
trail_json=$("$entire" trail resume "$selector" --no-resume --json 2>"$err_log") ||
	die "could not resolve trail $selector"

branch=$(printf '%s' "$trail_json" | jq -r '.trail.branch // empty')
title=$(printf '%s' "$trail_json" | jq -r '.trail.title // empty')
number=$(printf '%s' "$trail_json" | jq -r '.trail.number // empty')
[ -n "$branch" ] || die "trail $selector has no branch"

short_title=$(printf '%s' "$title" | cut -c1-46)
printf '  %strail #%s%s  %s\n' "$bold" "$number" "$reset" "$short_title"
printf '  %sbranch%s %s\n\n' "$dim" "$reset" "$branch"

# Agent picker. "none" leaves a plain shell in the new workspace.
index=1
choices=''
printf '  agent '
for kind in $AGENT_KINDS; do
	printf '%s[%s] %s%s ' "$dim" "$index" "$reset" "$kind"
	choices="$choices $index:$kind"
	index=$((index + 1))
done
printf '\n  choice %s[enter = %s]%s: ' "$dim" "$AGENT_DEFAULT" "$reset"
IFS= read -r choice || exit 0
case "$choice" in "$esc"*) exit 0 ;; esac

agent_kind=$AGENT_DEFAULT
if [ -n "$choice" ]; then
	agent_kind=''
	for pair in $choices; do
		case "$pair" in "$choice":*) agent_kind=${pair#*:} ;; esac
	done
	[ -n "$agent_kind" ] || die "no such choice: $choice"
fi
printf '\n'

label="#$number $(printf '%s' "$title" | cut -c1-28)"

# Re-opening beats failing: if the branch already has a worktree (from a previous
# run, or from `entire trail checkout --worktree`), adopt it instead.
existing=$("$herdr" worktree list --cwd "$repo_root" 2>"$err_log" |
	jq -r --arg b "$branch" '.result.worktrees[]? | select(.branch == $b) | .path' | head -n 1)

if [ -n "$existing" ]; then
	step "opening existing worktree $existing"
	response=$("$herdr" worktree open --cwd "$repo_root" --branch "$branch" \
		--label "$label" --focus 2>"$err_log") || die "worktree open failed"
	check_response "$response" "worktree open failed"
else
	# Herdr's worktree create only consults local refs — for a trail branch that
	# only exists on origin it would silently create a new branch from HEAD.
	if ! git show-ref --verify --quiet "refs/heads/$branch"; then
		step "fetching $branch from origin…"
		git fetch origin "refs/heads/$branch:refs/heads/$branch" >"$err_log" 2>&1 ||
			die "branch $branch not found locally or on origin"
	fi
	step "creating worktree for $branch…"
	response=$("$herdr" worktree create --cwd "$repo_root" --branch "$branch" \
		--label "$label" --focus 2>"$err_log") || die "worktree create failed"
	check_response "$response" "worktree create failed"
fi

checkout=$(printf '%s' "$response" | jq -r '.result.worktree.checkout_path // empty')
pane=$(printf '%s' "$response" | jq -r '.result.root_pane.pane_id // empty')
ok "${checkout:-worktree ready}"

if [ "$agent_kind" = "none" ] || [ -z "$pane" ]; then
	printf '\n'
	exit 0
fi

# An adopted workspace may already be running an agent in its root pane.
occupied=$("$herdr" agent list 2>/dev/null |
	jq -r --arg p "$pane" '[.result.agents[]? | select(.pane_id == $p)] | length')
if [ "${occupied:-0}" != "0" ]; then
	ok "$pane already has an agent"
	printf '\n'
	exit 0
fi

# Agent names must be unique among live agents and match [a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}.
name="trail-$number"
suffix=2
while [ "$suffix" -lt 20 ] &&
	"$herdr" agent list 2>/dev/null |
	jq -e --arg n "$name" '.result.agents[]? | select(.name == $n)' >/dev/null 2>&1; do
	name="trail-$number-$suffix"
	suffix=$((suffix + 1))
done

step "starting $agent_kind…"
if "$herdr" agent start "$name" --kind "$agent_kind" --pane "$pane" >"$err_log" 2>&1; then
	ok "$agent_kind running as $name in $pane"
	if [ -n "$INITIAL_PROMPT" ]; then
		text=$(printf '%s' "$INITIAL_PROMPT" |
			sed -e "s|{number}|$number|g" -e "s|{branch}|$branch|g" -e "s|{title}|$title|g")
		"$herdr" agent prompt "$name" "$text" >/dev/null 2>&1 ||
			printf '  %scould not send the initial prompt%s\n' "$dim" "$reset"
	fi
	printf '\n'
	exit 0
fi

# The worktree exists either way — an agent that would not start is worth
# reporting, but not worth discarding the workspace over.
printf '\n  %swarning%s %s did not start in %s\n' "$red" "$reset" "$agent_kind" "$pane"
sed -n '1,4p' "$err_log" 2>/dev/null | sed "s/^/  $dim/;s/\$/$reset/"
printf '\n  press enter to close '
read -r _ || true

input.content:
# Entire Trail Worktree

A Herdr plugin: paste an Entire trail id or URL, get a worktree workspace on
that trail's branch with an agent already running in it.

It's the `new worktree` flow (`prefix+shift+g`), except you name a trail instead
of a branch.

```
  new worktree from trail  entireio/cli

  trail (number, id, branch, or URL): https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1000
  trail #1000  Detect hook-config drift for every agent
  branch soph/pi-reenable

  agent [1] claude [2] codex [3] none
  choice [enter = claude]:

  creating worktree for soph/pi-reenable…
  ✓ /Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-pi-reenable
  starting claude…
  ✓ claude running as trail-1000 in wF:p1
```

## Install

```bash
herdr plugin link /path/to/herdr-plugin-trail-worktree
```

Then bind a key in `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`:

```toml
[[keys.command]]
key = "prefix+shift+e"
type = "plugin_action"
command = "entire.trail-worktree.new"
description = "new worktree from trail"
```

Requires `entire`, `git`, and `jq` on `PATH`, and Herdr 0.8.0+.

## What it does

1. Resolves the trail with `entire trail resume <selector> --no-resume --json`,
   which accepts a number, trail id, or branch and returns the branch and title.
   A pasted URL is reduced to its trail number first, and its `owner/repo` is
   checked against the workspace's `origin` — resolving a foreign trail here
   would silently check out the wrong branch.
2. Fetches the branch if it only exists on `origin`. This step matters: Herdr's
   own `worktree create --branch` consults local refs only, so without it a
   remote-only trail branch would silently become a *new* branch off `HEAD`.
3. Creates the worktree workspace with `herdr worktree create`, so the checkout
   lands under `worktrees.directory` (`~/.herdr/worktrees/<repo>/<slug>`) and is
   grouped with the parent repo workspace like any other Herdr worktree. If the
   branch already has a worktree, it re-opens that one instead of failing.
4. Starts the chosen agent in the new workspace's root pane, named `trail-<n>`
   so `herdr agent read trail-1000` and friends work.

Remove one with `herdr worktree remove --workspace <id>`, the same as any Herdr
worktree. The branch is never deleted.

## Entry points

The keybinding is the main one. The action also reads the terminal selection: if
you highlight a trail URL or a bare trail number before pressing the key, the
popup offers it as the default and you just press Enter.

You can also call it from a script or an agent:

```bash
herdr plugin action invoke entire.trail-worktree.new
```

Close the popup without doing anything with `ctrl+c`, `ctrl+d`, or `Esc` then
`Enter` (the popup passes Escape through to the script rather than closing on
it).

## Config

Optional, at `$(herdr plugin config-dir entire.trail-worktree)/config.env`:

```sh
# Agents offered in the picker, in order. "none" leaves a plain shell.
AGENT_KINDS="claude codex droid none"

# Pre-selected on Enter.
AGENT_DEFAULT="claude"

# Sent to the agent once it is ready. {number}, {branch} and {title} expand.
INITIAL_PROMPT="You are working on trail #{number} ({title}). Run 'entire trail show {number}' for context first."
```

Any Herdr agent kind works: `pi`, `claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `cursor`,
`opencode`, `copilot`, `droid`, `amp`, `grok`, and the rest of the list in
`herdr agent start --help`.

## Notes

- `entire trail checkout <n> --worktree` (Entire CLI, `main`) does a similar job
  outside Herdr, but places checkouts in `<repo>/.entire/worktrees` and does not
  open a workspace. This plugin deliberately uses Herdr's own worktree directory
  and lifecycle instead. Worktrees made either way are picked up by step 3, so
  the two coexist.
- The popup is the only way to accept pasted input: plugin actions take no
  arguments, and Herdr plugins have no native UI surface (no sidebar or menu
  entries).

tty_state=''

restore_tty() {
	[ -n "$tty_state" ] || return 0
	stty "$tty_state" 2>/dev/null
	tty_state=''
}

trap 'restore_tty' EXIT
trap 'restore_tty; exit 130' INT TERM

raw_on() {
	[ -t 0 ] || return 1
	tty_state=$(stty -g 2>/dev/null) || return 1
	stty -icanon -echo min 1 time 0 2>/dev/null || return 1
}

# Numeric value of one byte from stdin; empty on timeout. "peek" waits 100ms,
# anything else blocks.
read_byte() {
	[ "${1:-block}" != peek ] || stty min 0 time 1 2>/dev/null
	value=$(dd bs=1 count=1 2>/dev/null | od -An -tu1 | tr -dc '0-9')
	[ "${1:-block}" != peek ] || stty min 1 time 0 2>/dev/null
	printf '%s' "$value"
}

# Consumes the tail of a CSI/SS3 sequence after ESC and its introducer.
swallow_sequence() {
	case "$1" in
	91 | 79) ;;
	*) return 0 ;;
	esac
	while :; do
		tail_byte=$(read_byte peek)
		[ -n "$tail_byte" ] || return 0
		if [ "$tail_byte" -ge 64 ] && [ "$tail_byte" -le 126 ]; then
			return 0
		fi
	done
}

byte_to_char() { printf "\\$(printf '%03o' "$1")"; }

# Reads a line into REPLY_LINE. Returns 1 when cancelled (Escape, ctrl+c,
# ctrl+d). Falls back to a plain read when stdin is not a terminal.
read_line() {
	REPLY_LINE=''
	if ! raw_on; then
		IFS= read -r REPLY_LINE || return 1
		return 0
	fi
	while :; do
		byte=$(read_byte)
		[ -n "$byte" ] || continue
		case "$byte" in
		27)
			next=$(read_byte peek)
			if [ -z "$next" ]; then

				return 1
			fi
			swallow_sequence "$next"

		3 | 4)

			return 1

		8 | 127)

			fi
			;;
		21)

				REPLY_LINE=${REPLY_LINE%?}
				printf '\b \b'
			done
			;;
		*)
			if [ "$byte" -ge 32 ]; then
				char=$(byte_to_char "$byte")

				printf '%s' "$char"
			fi
			;;
		esac
	done

			fi

Fixed. Escape now cancels on the keypress.

**Why it was stuck:** two things compounding.

1. Herdr forwards *every* key to an open popup and has no close key of its own — `input/mod.rs:82` short-circuits all key handling into the popup's pty, so even the prefix key goes to the script. The only exits are the command exiting or a `popup.close` socket request.
2. My script read input with a line-buffered `read`, so Escape just parked a byte in the line buffer waiting for Enter.

`ctrl+c` did work (I verified it kills the script and closes the pane) — but that's not what anyone reaches for.

**The fix:** `bin/prompt.sh` now reads bytes in raw mode. A bare Escape is told apart from an arrow key (`ESC [ A`) by peeking for a follow-up byte with a 100 ms timeout. Backspace, `ctrl+u`, and `ctrl+c` work; the agent picker now takes a single keypress instead of a number plus Enter. Pastes are unaffected because herdr only wraps them in bracketed-paste markers when the app enabled DECSET 2004 (`pane.rs` `paste_payload`), which a shell script never does — so pasted URLs arrive as plain bytes.

Verified by driving a real pty with `pane send-keys`:

| input | result |
|---|---|
| bare `esc` at the trail prompt | closes |
| `esc` after typing `1000` | closes |
| arrow-up | stays open (sequence not mistaken for Escape) |
| `10009`, backspace, enter | resolves trail #1000 |
| `esc` at the agent picker | closes |
| single `9` at the picker, no Enter | `error no such choice: 9` |
| any key on the error screen | closes |

**Worth keeping in your back pocket:** if a popup from any plugin ever hangs, there's no CLI for it, but the socket method exists:

```bash
printf '{"id":"x","method":"popup.close","params":{}}\n' | nc -U "$HERDR_SOCKET_PATH"
```

I confirmed it responds (`popup_not_open` when nothing is open). That gap — popup-forwards-everything, no close key, no CLI for `popup.close` — looks like a reasonable upstream issue to file against herdr; a plugin author hitting it has no way to recover without knowing the raw socket.

No leftovers: worktree list and tabs are back to where they were, plugin still linked, `prefix+shift+E` still bound.

Here's the model, grounded in the source.

## What a plugin is

A directory with `herdr-plugin.toml` plus commands herdr can spawn. Herdr owns installation, manifest validation, keybindings, panes, events, and the socket API; the plugin owns its language, dependencies, and state. There is no SDK and no restricted command set — the entire herdr CLI is the plugin API, reached through `HERDR_BIN_PATH`. A plugin can do anything you can do at a shell.

## The six ways plugin code executes

| Declared as | Runs when | Who triggers it |
|---|---|---|
| `[[build]]` | during `plugin install`, after you confirm | install-time, once |
| `[[startup]]` | every server start + every live handoff | **nobody — automatic** |
| `[[events]]` | on `worktree.created`, `pane.agent_status_changed`, … | herdr, on activity |
| `[[actions]]` | keybinding, `plugin action invoke`, link handler | you, or anything with socket access |
| `[[panes]]` | `plugin pane open` | you, or an action |
| `[[link_handlers]]` | ctrl+click on a URL matching a regex | you, on **terminal content** |

`[[startup]]` is the one to read carefully in someone else's manifest: it is code that runs on every herdr start, forever, with no further interaction.

## Where things live

```
~/.config/herdr/plugins.json          registry: what's installed and enabled (global to your user)
~/.config/herdr/plugins/github/<id>/  managed checkouts from `plugin install`
~/.config/herdr/plugins/config/<id>/  HERDR_PLUGIN_CONFIG_DIR — your .env files
~/.local/state/herdr/plugins/<id>/    HERDR_PLUGIN_STATE_DIR — plugin runtime state
~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock            the API socket, mode 0600
```

Linked plugins stay where they are; only `install` copies anything.

## The trust boundary

**There isn't one around the plugin.** The boundary is your user account.

Plugin commands run as you, inherit your environment, get `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`, and can call the full CLI. Nothing is sandboxed, no capabilities are declared or enforced, and herdr does not read the code. The docs say this plainly, and the code matches it: `plugin_command.rs` just builds a `Command` and spawns it.

The socket is `0o600` (`server/socket_paths.rs:12`), so the perimeter is "processes running as your uid." Inside that perimeter there is no further checking — and that perimeter is wider than it looks, because **every agent in every pane is inside it**. `herdr` is on `PATH` and `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH` is in the pane environment.

Concretely, in this session: I ran `herdr plugin link <dir>` and it registered and enabled a plugin, no prompt, no preview. `plugin.link` is a socket method (`plugin.link`, `plugin.enable`, `plugin.unlink` are all in the API table) and the handler validates the manifest and saves the registry — there is no confirmation step anywhere in it. An agent that can write a directory can give itself persistent auto-run code on your machine.

## What herdr actually guarantees

The protections are real but narrow, and all sit at install time or spawn time:

- **`plugin install` previews and confirms** — `print_install_preview` lists every build, startup, action, event, and pane *command line*, plus the resolved commit, and asks `[y/N]`. `--yes` skips it. This is CLI-only; nothing on the socket path previews anything.
- **Build can't rewrite the manifest behind your back** — `ensure_manifest_unchanged_after_build` re-parses after building and aborts if it differs from what you approved. So a build step can't add a startup hook you never saw.
- **Commands are argv, never a shell string.** No shell expansion unless the plugin starts a shell itself.
- **Callers can't spoof herdr's env** — `panes.rs:244` strips any caller-supplied `HERDR_*` before injecting the real values, so `--env HERDR_SOCKET_PATH=...` can't redirect a plugin.
- **Version and platform gates** — `min_herdr_version` refuses a plugin needing a newer binary; `platforms` gates per item.
- **Config and state are separate from the checkout**, so reinstalling doesn't clobber your `.env` and your secrets don't live in a managed git checkout.

What the preview does *not* show is the content of what runs. `action new: ./bin/open-prompt.sh` tells you a script executes; it says nothing about what's in it. Reading the preview is not reading the plugin.

The [marketplace](https://herdr.dev/plugins/) is an automatic index of public repos tagged `herdr-plugin` whose manifests parse. Listing is not vetting.

## The one place untrusted data reaches plugin code

`HERDR_PLUGIN_CONTEXT_JSON` can carry `selected_text` and `clicked_url` — i.e. **terminal output**, which is attacker-influenced (a URL in a log line, text in a diff). Link handlers exist precisely to route clicked URLs into a plugin action.

Herdr passes these as environment variables, not argv, so there's no injection at the herdr layer. The risk lands entirely on the plugin author: a plugin doing `sh -c "$HERDR_PLUGIN_CLICKED_URL"` or `eval` on a selection is remotely triggerable by anything that can print to your terminal.

The trail plugin treats it as untrusted: the selection is only used if it matches `*/trails/[0-9]*` or is all digits, otherwise it's dropped (`bin/open-prompt.sh`), and it's only ever passed as a quoted `--env` value and pattern-matched — never evaluated.

## Practical rule

Treat a plugin like a shell profile you're sourcing from someone else's repo, not like a browser extension. Before `install` or `link`: read `herdr-plugin.toml`, look hardest at `[[startup]]`, then read the scripts it points at. Pin `--ref` for anything you don't control, since `install` re-clones and there's no `plugin update` — reinstalling is what pulls new code.

title: Persistence and remote access
description: Detach from Herdr, reattach later, use named sessions, and connect over SSH.
---

Herdr keeps panes running in a background server. Your terminal client can detach and reconnect later.

For the local, SSH, and `herdr --remote` workflows, see [How to work with Herdr](/docs/how-to-work/).

## Detach and reattach

Detach the client with `ctrl+b q`; panes and agents keep running. Reattach by running `herdr` again. Stop the session and its panes with `herdr server stop`.

When Herdr starts again after a full server stop, it restores the saved session shape. For what survives detach, server restart, screen history replay, native agent session restore, and live handoff, see [Session state and restore](/docs/session-state/).

## Named sessions

Use named sessions when you want independent Herdr servers.

```bash
herdr session list
herdr session attach work
herdr session attach side-project
herdr session stop work
herdr session delete side-project
```

A named session has its own panes, tabs, workspaces, sockets, and runtime state. It still shares the same global config file.

Use `--json` for scripts:

```bash
herdr session list --json
herdr session stop work --json
herdr session delete side-project --json
```

## Remote attach over SSH

Herdr supports two remote modes. [How to work with Herdr](/docs/how-to-work/) compares them. SSH to the server and run `herdr` there for the tmux-style path, or attach through SSH from your local machine:

```bash
herdr --remote workbox
herdr --remote ssh://you@server:2222
```

In this mode, your local Herdr is a thin client. It connects over SSH, starts or attaches to the remote Herdr server, and streams the UI back to your local terminal. Because the client runs locally, Herdr can bridge local desktop features such as image clipboard paste into the remote session by copying the image to a remote temp file and pasting that path.

By default, `herdr --remote` uses your local Herdr keybindings for that attach. This keeps local muscle memory even when the remote server has different config. The local keybindings are a snapshot from attach time; detach and reattach after editing local keybindings. Use `--remote-keybindings server` when you want the remote server config instead. Local custom command keybindings are not sent, because those commands would run on the remote host.

For repeat targets, use your SSH config:

```text
Host workbox
  HostName server.example.com
  User you
  Port 2222
```

Then attach with:

```bash
herdr --remote workbox
```

Remote attach supports Linux, macOS, and Windows local clients connecting to Linux or macOS hosts on x86_64 and aarch64. Herdr checks the remote platform, prefers a matching `herdr` already on the remote `PATH`, then checks common direct, Homebrew, mise, and Nix profile install paths. If no matching binary exists, interactive runs prompt to install one to `~/.local/bin/herdr`; non-interactive runs fail instead of modifying the host. If `~/.local/bin` is not on the remote `PATH`, Herdr warns after install. Windows is not supported as the remote host.

By default, `herdr --remote` runs remote setup and the bridge through a temporary SSH config that includes your SSH config first, then adds fallback keepalive settings. Existing user keepalive settings win. Linux and macOS clients also use a private per-attach control socket for connection reuse; Windows OpenSSH does not. Set `[remote].manage_ssh_config = false` to use plain `ssh` without Herdr's generated config or control socket.

Remote attach uses your normal OpenSSH authentication. If the target uses a passphrase-protected key in a non-interactive shell, script, CI job, or mobile terminal that cannot show the passphrase prompt, load the key into ssh-agent first:

```bash
ssh-add
herdr --remote workbox
```

For any remote authentication failure, verify plain SSH access first with `ssh workbox`, then run `herdr --remote workbox` again.

Short answer: **on the server host** — the machine where the herdr server runs. Not on your laptop.

With `herdr --remote workbox`, your local herdr is a thin client that streams UI. Everything plugin-related lives server-side: the registry it reads is the server's `~/.config/herdr/plugins.json`, the action/pane/startup commands are spawned by the server process, and plugin panes are server panes. Your local `plugins.json` is inert for that session. So:

```bash
ssh workbox
herdr plugin link ~/src/herdr-plugin-trail-worktree   # or plugin install owner/repo
```

`herdr plugin ...` talks to whatever socket is local to *that* CLI process, and `plugin.link` resolves its `path` on the server's filesystem — so running it from your laptop against a remote session isn't a thing; ssh in and run it there.

**Two things that will bite you:**

**1. The keybinding needs to be in the remote config *and* you need `--remote-keybindings server`.** By default `--remote` sends your local keybindings, and `[[keys.command]]` entries are stripped from that profile on the way out (`config.rs:151`, test name: `local_keybindings_profile_includes_defaults_and_excludes_commands`) — the docs justify it as "those commands would run on the remote host." Worse, the client profile *replaces* the server's set rather than merging (`headless.rs:1186` `unwrap_or(&self.server_keybindings)`), and `parse_client_keybindings` does `config.keys.command.clear()`. Net effect: on a default remote attach, **no custom command keybindings are active at all** — not yours, not the server's. So `prefix+shift+E` does nothing.

```bash
herdr --remote workbox --remote-keybindings server
```

That, plus the `[[keys.command]]` block in the *remote* `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`, makes it work. The action is always reachable regardless via `herdr plugin action invoke entire.trail-worktree.new` from a pane.

The other remote style — ssh in and just run `herdr` there — has none of this caveat, since the server config is used directly.

**2. This particular plugin's dependencies are all remote-side.** `entire`, `git`, and `jq` must be on the remote host, `entire` must be logged in there, the repo clone must be there, and the worktree lands under the *remote's* `worktrees.directory`. Nothing reaches back to your laptop.

`~/.config/herdr/herdr-server.log`, every `agent.start` since you started using this:

2026-08-13T13:22:50  started → ok     (13ms)
```

4 of 7 failed — and every failure came back in **1–3 milliseconds**. A real 30-second timeout can't do that. The request is being rejected outright. The 13:22 pair is the clearest: failed, you retried 45s later, it worked.

I reproduced the exact error:

```
$ herdr agent start testname --kind claude --pane wE:p1
{"error":{"code":"agent_pane_busy","message":"agent target pane wE:p1 is not an available shell"}}
```

## Why

`agent start` demands that the pane's shell be the **sole** process in its foreground process group (`platform/mod.rs:223`, `available_pane_shell_from_job` — it returns `None` if *any* process in the job isn't the shell itself). The worktree workspace is a second or two old when the plugin calls it, so the shell is usually still working through its rc files — mise, direnv, completions, prompt setup. During that window the pane is "busy" and herdr says no instantly. A moment later the prompt lands and it works, which is why a retry always fixes it.

So it's a startup race in my plugin, not a claude problem and not a herdr bug. The wording just misleads: "did not start" reads like a timeout. (There *is* a genuine 30s timeout — CLI-side, message `timed out waiting for agent startup` — but you're not hitting it; those would show as `outcome="ok"` on the server and take 30s.)

## Fixed

- **Retries `agent start` once a second while the error is `agent_pane_busy`**, up to `AGENT_START_ATTEMPTS` (default 15, configurable). Any other error fails immediately — no masking of real problems. Verified the loop against a genuinely busy pane: 3 attempts, correct classification, correct give-up.
- **Stopped destroying the evidence.** The old code truncated one log per run, so a failure was erased by your next attempt — that's why `last-error.log` was empty when I looked. Now it appends to a rolling `history.log` (400-line cap) at `~/.local/state/herdr/plugins/<id>/history.log`, with timestamps and each attempt's error.
- The failure message now names the error code, points at the log, and prints the exact `herdr agent start …` command to run by hand.

Ran the full flow after the change: worktree created, claude started as `trail-1000` first try, no retries needed. Test worktree removed. Since the race is intermittent I can't force a real-world miss on demand — the retry loop itself is verified in isolation, not in a naturally-occurring race.

Yes — private works, but not with your current git setup. I tested it.

## What `plugin install` actually does

`src/cli/plugin.rs:835`:

```
git init
git remote add origin https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git    ← hardcoded HTTPS
git fetch --depth 1 origin HEAD                            ← or your --ref
git checkout --detach FETCH_HEAD
```

Two consequences:

- The URL is **always HTTPS** (`remote_url()`, line 754). The shorthand parser explicitly rejects full URLs and `git@…` forms, so there's no way to ask for SSH.
- There's no herdr-specific auth. It's just `git`, so whatever credentials git has are the credentials install has. Private repos are supported in exactly the sense that `git clone https://github.com/org/private` is supported.

## Your setup would fail today

I replicated that exact sequence against `entireio/entire-ci`:

```
fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com': Device not configured
```

Your global `credential.helper` is `osxkeychain`, but there's no GitHub HTTPS credential in it — all your remotes are `git@github.com:`, so you've never needed one. Install also runs git with stdin closed, so it can't fall back to asking.

Each teammate needs one of these once:

1. **`gh auth setup-git`** — makes `gh` the credential helper for github.com. Easiest to tell people to run, and most of your org already has `gh`.
2. **A PAT in the keychain** — `git credential-osxkeychain store` with a token that has `repo` scope.
3. **Rewrite HTTPS to SSH globally** — works with the SSH keys people already have:
   ```bash
   git config --global url."git@github.com:".insteadOf "https://github.com/"
   ```
   I verified this one against the same private repo: fetch succeeded, `FETCH_HEAD` resolved. Caveat: it's global and silently redirects *every* HTTPS github.com clone to SSH, which surprises people later.

Whichever they pick, `herdr plugin install entireio/herdr-plugin-trail-worktree` then works normally.

## Other things that follow from private

- **No marketplace listing.** The index only crawls public repos tagged `herdr-plugin`, so discovery is word-of-mouth — fine, since the install command is one line.
- **`--ref` still works** and is worth using in the instructions you hand out: install re-fetches on every reinstall and there's no `plugin update`, so pinning a tag is how you control what teammates run.
- **Org SSO.** If entireio enforces SAML SSO, a PAT must be explicitly authorized for the org, otherwise it 404s in a way that reads like "repo doesn't exist." `gh auth setup-git` sidesteps this.
- **Nothing about this changes the trust story** — teammates are running your scripts as themselves, and `install` shows them the command list before it runs anything.

One caveat on the plugin itself before you hand it out: it hardcodes `entire`, `git`, and `jq`, and assumes `entire` is logged in. `jq` in particular isn't installed by default on macOS before 15 — the script fails with a clear message, but you may want it in the README's prerequisites, which it currently is.
